Solving Absolute Value Inequalities.name: Solving Absolute Value Inequalities

parameters.name: form
parameters.description: the absolute-value inequality form, e.g., |x - c| < d

parameters.name: variable
parameters.description: the variable contained in the absolute value

Solving Absolute Value Inequalities.description: Translate an inequality involving an absolute value into a simple interval bound for the variable.
cues: problem involves an inequality with an absolute value
the solution set is a contiguous interval for the variable
implementation: rewrite |variable - center| < bound as -bound < variable - center < bound
deduce the solution interval for variable: (center - bound, center + bound)

Squaring Nonnegative Quantities to Compa.name: Squaring Nonnegative Quantities to Compare

parameters.name: left
parameters.description: left-hand nonnegative expression

parameters.name: right
parameters.description: right-hand nonnegative expression

Squaring Nonnegative Quantities to Compa.description: Use the monotonicity of the squaring function on nonnegative numbers to compare expressions and simplify inequalities.
cues: comparing two nonnegative quantities (e.g., absolute values)
the problem reduces to an inequality that becomes linear after squaring
implementation: verify both sides are nonnegative
apply the equivalence a < b iff a^2 < b^2 for nonnegative a, b
simplify to obtain the resulting inequality or range

Arithmetic Series / Sum of Consecutive I.name: Arithmetic Series / Sum of Consecutive Integers

parameters.name: start
parameters.description: first term in the consecutive range

parameters.name: end
parameters.description: last term in the consecutive range

Arithmetic Series / Sum of Consecutive I.description: The sum of a consecutive integer interval from start to end is (start + end) times the number of terms divided by 2.
cues: the solution set forms a consecutive integer interval
you need the total sum of all integers in that interval
implementation: n = end - start + 1
sum = n * (start + end) / 2

Intersection of Constraint Solution Sets.name: Intersection of Constraint Solution Sets

parameters.name: constraints
parameters.description: list of individual inequality constraints

Intersection of Constraint Solution Sets.description: Solve multiple independent inequalities and take the intersection of their solution sets to obtain the final feasible set.
cues: problem imposes several inequalities on the same variable
feasible solutions must satisfy all constraints simultaneously
multiple independent digit-length constraints are imposed on the same variable
the solution set is the intersection of two (or more) intervals
problem imposes multiple domain constraints from different radical expressions
domain equals the common feasible set satisfying all constraints
implementation: determine the solution set for each constraint
final solution set = intersection of all individual solution sets
translate each constraint into an interval
compute the intersection of these intervals to obtain the feasible range
Solve each constraint independently to obtain its domain
take the intersection of all per-constraint domains to obtain the final domain

Viète's Formulas.name: Viète's Formulas

parameters.name: polynomial
parameters.description: monic polynomial whose roots are r_i

parameters.name: degree
parameters.description: the degree n of the polynomial

parameters.name: constant_term
parameters.description: the constant term of the polynomial

Viète's Formulas.description: relate sums and products of the roots of a polynomial to its coefficients
cues: problem involves a polynomial with known roots and asks for a sum over those roots
need to extract the sum of the roots from coefficients without solving for the roots
polynomial is monic
product of roots is tied to the constant term via Viète's relations
implementation: identify the coefficient corresponding to the x^{n-1} term to obtain sum of roots
compute sum of roots = - (leading coefficient's next coefficient) / (leading coefficient)
for a monic P of degree n, r_1 r_2 ... r_n = (−1)^n * constant_term
similarly, sums of roots correspond to coefficients with alternating signs

Logarithmic derivative of a polynomial.name: Logarithmic derivative of a polynomial

parameters.name: P
parameters.description: polynomial with roots r_i

parameters.name: a
parameters.description: shift value chosen to simplify the sum

Logarithmic derivative of a polynomial.description: use P'(a)/P(a) = sum_i 1/(a - r_i) to convert sums over roots into evaluations of P and its derivative
cues: problem asks for a sum of terms of the form 1/(r_i + a)
desire to transform a root-sum into a computable ratio of derivatives
implementation: compute P(a) and P'(a)
apply P'(a)/P(a) = sum_i 1/(a - r_i)
rearrange to obtain sum_i 1/(r_i + a) as needed

Rational decomposition of functions of r.name: Rational decomposition of functions of roots

parameters.name: f
parameters.description: expression in r that needs summation

Rational decomposition of functions of r.description: rewrite a function of a root as a sum of a polynomial part and a simple rational part to simplify summation
cues: target expression in r can be split into parts easier to sum separately
enables applying different summation tools to each part
implementation: find an identity expressing f(r) = g(r) + h(r) where g is a polynomial in r and h is a simple term
sum g(r_i) using Viète's results or symmetric sums
sum h(r_i) using an appropriate technique (e.g., logarithmic derivative or direct evaluation)

Factor Theorem.name: Factor Theorem
Factor Theorem.description: If a polynomial evaluates to zero at a, then (x − a) is a factor; used to infer a product of linear factors from zeros.
cues: the auxiliary polynomial has zeros at multiple distinct input values
the polynomial’s degree is bounded (e.g., not exceeding a given degree)
implementation: from the zeros, conclude the polynomial is divisible by the product of (x − r_i)
use the leading coefficient to fix any remaining constant factor and obtain the full factorization

Monic Root Factorization.name: Monic Root Factorization

parameters.name: roots
parameters.description: the roots of the polynomial

parameters.name: degree
parameters.description: the degree of the polynomial

Monic Root Factorization.description: A monic polynomial of a given degree with a prescribed set of roots equals the product ∏(x − root_i); used to reconstruct the polynomial from its roots.
cues: the polynomial is known to be monic
the number of distinct roots matches the degree
implementation: write the polynomial as a product ∏(x − root_i)
since it is monic, no extra constant factor is needed; validate by checking the leading term

Auxiliary Polynomial Construction.name: Auxiliary Polynomial Construction
Auxiliary Polynomial Construction.description: Define an auxiliary polynomial Q(x) = P(x) − target(x) to force specified values to become zeros; then analyze Q to recover P.
cues: given equalities P(k) = target(k) for several inputs
strategy involves forming Q(x) = P(x) − target(x) to induce zeros
implementation: form Q(x) = P(x) − target(x)
deduce zeros of Q at the specified inputs
factor Q using root-based reasoning and match leading coefficients to recover P

Im(AB) = 0 Real-Product Constraint.name: Im(AB) = 0 Real-Product Constraint

parameters.name: A
parameters.description: fixed complex constant multiplied by the variable part B

Im(AB) = 0 Real-Product Constraint.description: enforce that the product of two complex quantities is real by setting its imaginary part to zero and substituting known fixed parts.
cues: AB is constrained to be real
A is a fixed nonzero complex constant
implementation: Let B be a variable complex expression; compute Im(A·B) and set it to 0.
Substitute real and imaginary parts of A and B; isolate a locus equation in the real variables defining z.

Möbius Transformation Locus.name: Möbius Transformation Locus

parameters.name: z2
parameters.description: fixed complex point used in B's numerator

parameters.name: z3
parameters.description: fixed complex point used in B's denominator

Möbius Transformation Locus.description: interpret the ratio B = (z − z2)/(z − z3) as a Möbius map and determine the preimage of a fixed line through the origin, which yields a circle or line in the z-plane.
cues: B is defined as (z − z2)/(z − z3)
AB being real implies B lies on a line through the origin in the B-plane
implementation: Fix the target line in the B-plane (through the origin); invert the Möbius map to obtain the locus of z in the z-plane.
Identify whether the resulting locus is a circle or a line and determine its parameters.

Completing the Square to Identify a Circ.name: Completing the Square to Identify a Circle

parameters.name: equation
parameters.description: the general quadratic expression in x and y

Completing the Square to Identify a Circ.description: transform a quadratic in x and y into the standard circle form by completing the square to read off the center and radius.
cues: Equation begins with x^2 + y^2 plus linear terms
After rearrangement, a circle form (x−h)^2 + (y−k)^2 = R^2 emerges
implementation: Group x-terms and y-terms, complete the square for each, and identify the circle center (h, k) and radius R from the constant term.

Extremum on a Circle (Topmost Point).name: Extremum on a Circle (Topmost Point)

parameters.name: center
parameters.description: circle center coordinates (h, k)

parameters.name: radius
parameters.description: circle radius

Extremum on a Circle (Topmost Point).description: to maximize the imaginary part on a circular locus, take the topmost point of the circle (align x with the center and add the radius to the y-coordinate).
cues: Locus is a circle in the z-plane
Objective is to maximize the imaginary part (y-coordinate)
implementation: Set x = h and y = k + R to obtain the topmost point; read off the corresponding z = x + i y.

Polynomial Resultant Trick.name: Polynomial Resultant Trick

parameters.name: polynomial
parameters.description: the monic polynomial P with roots r_i

parameters.name: shift
parameters.description: the form of the shift in the second polynomial, e.g., P(u − x)

parameters.name: evaluation_point
parameters.description: the value(s) at which the resultant is specialized (e.g., u = 0)

Polynomial Resultant Trick.description: Use the resultant of a polynomial with a shifted version to encode products over sums/differences of its roots; specialize the resultant to extract target symmetric products.
cues: problem constructs Res_x(P(x), P(u − x))
the resultant is expressed as ∏ P(u − r_i) and also as ∏_{i,j} (u − (r_i + r_j))
specialization yields a product over all pairwise sums of roots
implementation: recall that if P is monic with roots r_i, then Res_x(P(x), Q(x)) = ∏ Q(r_i)
for Q(x) = P(u − x), obtain Res_x(P(x), P(u − x)) = ∏_{i,j} (u − (r_i + r_j))
specialize to the chosen evaluation_point to read off the desired symmetric product

Pairwise Sum Product Decomposition.name: Pairwise Sum Product Decomposition

parameters.name: roots
parameters.description: the set of roots {r_i}

parameters.name: K
parameters.description: the product over unordered pairs K = ∏_{i<j} (r_i + r_j)

Pairwise Sum Product Decomposition.description: Express the full product over all ordered pairs of sums of roots in terms of the product over unordered pair sums and the product over diagonal terms.
cues: need to relate ∏_{i,j} (r_i + r_j) to K
there are diagonal terms (i = j) and off-diagonal terms (i ≠ j)
implementation: observe that for i ≠ j, (r_i + r_j) appears twice (as (i,j) and (j,i)); for i = j, term is 2 r_i
deduce the relation ∏_{i,j} (r_i + r_j) = K^2 · ∏_{i=1}^n (2 r_i)

Base-b Digit Count Range.name: Base-b Digit Count Range

parameters.name: base
parameters.description: the base b

parameters.name: digits
parameters.description: the number of digits k

Base-b Digit Count Range.description: The k-digit numbers in base b satisfy b^(k-1) ≤ n ≤ b^k − 1.
cues: problem states a number has k digits in base b
bounds can be expressed via powers of b
implementation: set lower_bound = b^(digits − 1)
set upper_bound = b^digits − 1
feasible n lie in [lower_bound, upper_bound]

Midpoint of Consecutive Integer Interval.name: Midpoint of Consecutive Integer Interval

parameters.name: a
parameters.description: left endpoint

parameters.name: b
parameters.description: right endpoint

Midpoint of Consecutive Integer Interval.description: For a consecutive integer interval [a, b], the midpoint is (a + b)/2 and often identifies the central value of the set
cues: feasible set forms an inclusive range of consecutive integers
implementation: compute midpoint m = (a + b) / 2
if the number of terms is odd, m is the unique middle element
if even, m is the average of the two middle elements (used as center)

LCM-based Periodicity Reduction.name: LCM-based Periodicity Reduction

parameters.name: moduli
parameters.description: the two moduli governing the separate residue conditions

LCM-based Periodicity Reduction.description: When two conditions depend on residues modulo different integers, combine them into a single period equal to the least common multiple to analyze once and scale.
cues: problem has two independent residue conditions (mod a and mod b)
counting over a large range with a repeating pattern
implementation: compute L = lcm(a, b)
analyze the set of good indices within one period 1..L
total_good = floor(N / L) * good_per_period
handle remaining indices in the partial tail 1..(N mod L)

Single-Period Enumeration.name: Single-Period Enumeration

parameters.name: period_length
parameters.description: length of the repeating block (the LCM of moduli)

Single-Period Enumeration.description: Within one complete period, enumerate all indices that satisfy the combined condition to obtain the per-period count.
cues: a period length has been identified
need the count of satisfying indices within a full period
implementation: for n = 1 to period_length, test the combined condition
count how many n satisfy C(n) = S(n) within the period
optionally record the residue classes that work for tail analysis

Residue Pair Mapping for Combined Condit.name: Residue Pair Mapping for Combined Conditions

parameters.name: moduli
parameters.description: the two moduli governing the separate residue constraints

Residue Pair Mapping for Combined Condit.description: Build a cross-tabulation of residues modulo each modulus to identify which residue pairs satisfy the combined requirement.
cues: combined condition depends on two independent residue properties
need to translate a global condition into local residue pairs
implementation: construct a table with rows representing residues mod a and columns residues mod b
mark cells where the pair (n mod a, n mod b) satisfies the target
translate good cells back to the global indices modulo L

Integer Interval Cardinality via Floor a.name: Integer Interval Cardinality via Floor and Ceiling

parameters.name: a
parameters.description: lower real endpoint of the interval

parameters.name: b
parameters.description: upper real endpoint of the interval

Integer Interval Cardinality via Floor a.description: count integers in a real interval by converting endpoints to integer bounds using ceiling for the lower end and floor for the upper end
cues: problem asks for the number of integers n with a ≤ n ≤ b
endpoints are real numbers and must be converted to integer bounds
the appropriate bounds are ⌈a⌉ for the lower end and ⌊b⌋ for the upper end
implementation: compute lower = ⌈a⌉
compute upper = ⌊b⌋
if lower ≤ upper, answer = upper − lower + 1
otherwise, answer = 0

Monochromatic Orbits under Group Action.name: Monochromatic Orbits under Group Action

parameters.name: group
parameters.description: symmetry group acting on the domain

parameters.name: orbits
parameters.description: partition of the domain into orbits under the group action

Monochromatic Orbits under Group Action.description: Under a symmetry group acting on a grid, an invariant coloring must assign the same color to every element within each orbit; the count of invariant colorings equals 2^(number of orbits).
cues: problem asks for colorings invariant under all symmetries of a square (D4)
the action partitions the cells into orbits
invariant colorings require monochromatic orbits
implementation: compute the orbits of the domain under the group's action
assign a color to each orbit independently
total invariant colorings = 2^(number_of_orbits)
to enforce additional color constraints, apply complementary counting on top

Complementary Counting for Enforcing Col.name: Complementary Counting for Enforcing Color Variety

parameters.name: constraint
parameters.description: the constraint (e.g., "both colors appear")

Complementary Counting for Enforcing Col.description: To ensure both colors appear, count all invariant colorings and subtract the colorings that violate the condition (e.g., monochromatic colorings).
cues: there is a requirement that at least one square of each color
solution uses subtracting monochromatic cases
implementation: evaluate the total number of colorings that respect the symmetry
subtract the number of colorings that violate the constraint (commonly the all-one-color cases)

Orbit Classification under D4 on Centere.name: Orbit Classification under D4 on Centered Grid

parameters.name: coordinate_basis
parameters.description: center-relative coordinates (dx, dy)

parameters.name: orbit_signature
parameters.description: unordered pair of absolute magnitudes {abs(dx), abs(dy)}

Orbit Classification under D4 on Centere.description: Classify each cell by its orbit under the D4 symmetry group using center-relative coordinates; two cells share an orbit iff their center-relative absolute coordinate magnitudes form the same unordered pair.
cues: orbit determined by (|dx|, |dy|) up to order
coordinates are taken relative to the grid center
D4 maps cells by rotations/reflections preserving center
implementation: for each cell, compute (dx, dy) relative to center
compute a and b as the nonnegative magnitudes |dx|, |dy| and form the unordered pair {a,b}
group cells by identical {a,b} to obtain the orbit partition
number_of_orbits = number of distinct unordered pairs
invariant colorings = 2^(number_of_orbits)

LCM Congruence Lifting.name: LCM Congruence Lifting

parameters.name: moduli
parameters.description: the two moduli (m1, m2) involved

LCM Congruence Lifting.description: if two congruences share the same remainder modulo two moduli, they combine to a single congruence modulo the lcm of the moduli
cues: problem has two simultaneous congruences n ≡ s (mod m1) and n ≡ s (mod m2) with the same s
implementation: compute L = lcm(m1, m2)
conclude n ≡ s (mod L)

Residue-Block Counting in a Period.name: Residue-Block Counting in a Period

parameters.name: modulus
parameters.description: period length

parameters.name: allowed_residues
parameters.description: set of residues within a period that satisfy the condition

Residue-Block Counting in a Period.description: partition the integers into periods of length equal to the lcm of the moduli and count how many residues in each period satisfy the condition
cues: counting reduces to complete periods plus a possible partial period
there is a fixed count of valid residues per full period
implementation: determine number of complete periods in the interval
multiply by the per-period count of valid residues
count valid residues in the leftover partial period and add

Partial-Block Handling in Periodic Count.name: Partial-Block Handling in Periodic Counting
Partial-Block Handling in Periodic Count.description: manage leading and trailing partial blocks when the counting interval does not align with period boundaries
cues: interval boundaries do not align with period boundaries
implementation: count eligible numbers in the leading partial block
count eligible numbers in the trailing partial block
add the full-block counts in between

Median Slope Constraint.name: Median Slope Constraint

parameters.name: slope_of_median
parameters.description: the given slope value of the median from the vertex to the opposite side

Median Slope Constraint.description: Use the slope from a vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side to derive a linear relation among vertex coordinates.
cues: M is the midpoint of BC
slope of AM is specified
implementation: compute M as the midpoint of BC
set (y_A - y_M)/(x_A - x_M) equal to the given slope
solve the resulting equation to obtain a linear relation between the vertex coordinates

Triangle Area via Base-Height.name: Triangle Area via Base-Height

parameters.name: base_length
parameters.description: length of the chosen base

parameters.name: height
parameters.description: perpendicular distance from the opposite vertex to the base

Triangle Area via Base-Height.description: The area of a triangle equals one-half the product of a chosen base length and the corresponding height.
cues: area of triangle is given
base length is computable from the base endpoints
Use base-height formula for triangle area; choose a base side and compute the perpendicular distance from the opposite vertex to the base line
The base is a side of the triangle lying on a known line, so the height is the distance from the opposite vertex to that line
implementation: height = (2 * area) / base_length
Select a base side and compute its length
Compute the height as the perpendicular distance from the opposite vertex to the line containing the base
Area = (1/2) * base * height

Point-to-Line Distance Formula.name: Point-to-Line Distance Formula

parameters.name: line_A
parameters.description: coefficient A in line equation

parameters.name: line_B
parameters.description: coefficient B

parameters.name: line_C
parameters.description: constant term

parameters.name: line_coefficients
parameters.description: (A, B, C) in the line equation Ax + By + C = 0

parameters.name: point
parameters.description: Coordinates (x0, y0) of the point whose distance to the line is sought

Point-to-Line Distance Formula.description: The perpendicular distance from a point to a line Ax + By + C = 0 is |Ax0 + By0 + C| / sqrt(A^2 + B^2).
cues: need to relate a point's distance to a given line
the distance must equal a previously computed height
Height in a triangle can be obtained as the perpendicular distance from a vertex to the base line
The base line is given (or implicit) by a linear equation; compute the distance from the opposite vertex to this line
implementation: compute distance = |A*x0 + B*y0 + C| / sqrt(A^2 + B^2)
set distance equal to the height to generate an equation
Substitute the point into the distance formula to obtain the perpendicular distance
Use the result as the height in the base-height area computation

Solving Absolute Value Equations.name: Solving Absolute Value Equations

parameters.name: expression
parameters.description: the expression inside the absolute value

parameters.name: value
parameters.description: the nonnegative value on the right-hand side

Solving Absolute Value Equations.description: If |E| = k with k ≥ 0, solve by splitting into E = k and E = -k, yielding up to two linear equations.
cues: equation has an absolute value equated to a constant
implementation: form two equations: expression = value and expression = -value
solve each case, collect valid solutions

Reciprocal Polynomial Factorization (Pal.name: Reciprocal Polynomial Factorization (Palindromic Quartic)

parameters.name: a
parameters.description: the symmetric linear coefficient to be determined

Reciprocal Polynomial Factorization (Pal.description: Factor a reciprocal/palindromic polynomial by seeking a factorization into conjugate-linear-term quadratics that cancel odd-power terms.
cues: polynomial in the substitution variable has only even-power terms
coefficients are symmetric (palindromic)
anticipate a factorization of the form (t^2 + a t + 1)(t^2 - a t + 1)
implementation: assume factorization of the palindromic quartic into two quadratics with opposite linear terms
expand and equate coefficients to solve for a

Power Substitution to Reduce Degree.name: Power Substitution to Reduce Degree

parameters.name: substitution
parameters.description: the substitution relation (e.g., y = x^2)

Power Substitution to Reduce Degree.description: Use a substitution to reduce the degree of a polynomial, turning a high-degree problem into a lower-degree one.
cues: original polynomial in x has only even-power terms
you replace x^2 by a new variable to get a lower-degree polynomial
implementation: perform the substitution to obtain a lower-degree polynomial in the new variable
solve or factor the resulting polynomial

Coefficient Matching to Determine Factor.name: Coefficient Matching to Determine Factorization Parameters

parameters.name: unknowns
parameters.description: the variables/parameters to solve for in the factorization

Coefficient Matching to Determine Factor.description: Determine unknown coefficients in a factorization by expanding and matching coefficients term-by-term.
cues: you expand a proposed factorization and compare coefficients to derive equations for the unknowns
there is a small number of unknown parameters
implementation: write the product of proposed factors
equate coefficients of like powers to form a system of equations
solve for the unknown parameters

Squarefree Kernel of n.name: Squarefree Kernel of n

parameters.name: n
parameters.description: a positive integer

Squarefree Kernel of n.description: The squarefree part k in the unique factorization n = s^2 * k, where k is squarefree (no prime appears with exponent ≥ 2 in k).
cues: factor n into a square factor and a squarefree remainder
the squarefree part encodes which primes appear to odd exponent in n
implementation: Compute k by taking the product of primes appearing to an odd exponent in n (i.e., n = s^2 * k with k squarefree)
Note: k is zero if n = 0; otherwise k > 0

Even Exponent Criterion for Perfect Squa.name: Even Exponent Criterion for Perfect Squares
Even Exponent Criterion for Perfect Squa.description: An integer is a perfect square iff every prime's exponent in its prime factorization is even.
cues: to check if a product is a square, ensure all prime exponents are even
implementation: Factor the number; verify all exponents are even; if any exponent is odd, the number is not a square

Bound via sqrt in square-factor parametr.name: Bound via sqrt in square-factor parametrization

parameters.name: base factor
parameters.description: the coefficient multiplying the square of an integer

parameters.name: upper bound
parameters.description: the maximum allowed value of n

Bound via sqrt in square-factor parametr.description: If a number n is expressed as n = base * t^2 with integer t, then an upper bound on n yields an upper bound on t via t ≤ floor(sqrt(upper_bound / base)).
cues: n is written as base * t^2
there is an upper limit on n
implementation: Compute t_max = floor(sqrt(upper_bound / base)); enumerate t = 1 to t_max to generate all feasible n = base * t^2

Residue Class Parameterization.name: Residue Class Parameterization

parameters.name: modulus
parameters.description: m in the congruence n ≡ a (mod m)

parameters.name: residue
parameters.description: a in the congruence n ≡ a (mod m)

Residue Class Parameterization.description: Express numbers in a fixed residue class modulo m as n = a + m·k, turning a congruence constraint into a linear parameterization to analyze feasible k.
cues: problem requires selecting numbers belonging to a specific residue class modulo a modulus
objective is to maximize/minimize such a number within a bounded range
implementation: set n = residue + modulus · k
translate the given range for n into a range for k
determine feasible k and compute the extremal n from those k

Integer Bound via Floor and Ceiling.name: Integer Bound via Floor and Ceiling

parameters.name: lower_bound
parameters.description: real lower bound for the parameter

parameters.name: upper_bound
parameters.description: real upper bound for the parameter

Integer Bound via Floor and Ceiling.description: Convert a real-valued interval for an integer parameter into an integer interval using ceiling for the lower bound and floor for the upper bound.
cues: the parameter of interest must be an integer
feasible values form a real interval
implementation: compute k_min = ⌈lower_bound⌉
compute k_max = ⌊upper_bound⌋
enumerate or select among integers k with k_min ≤ k ≤ k_max

Shoelace Formula for Polygon Area.name: Shoelace Formula for Polygon Area

parameters.name: vertex list
parameters.description: ordered vertices of the polygon around its boundary

Shoelace Formula for Polygon Area.description: Compute area of a polygon from vertex coordinates using the shoelace determinant
cues: problem provides a polygon via a sequence of coordinate points
area can be obtained directly from the vertex coordinates
implementation: compute sum1 = sum over i of x_i * y_{i+1} (indices modulo n)
compute sum2 = sum over i of y_i * x_{i+1} (indices modulo n)
area = 0.5 * |sum1 - sum2|

Triangulation into Triangles for Area.name: Triangulation into Triangles for Area
Triangulation into Triangles for Area.description: Decompose a polygon into triangles along a diagonal and sum their areas
cues: region of interest is a simple polygon defined by multiple vertices
a diagonal can split the region into non-overlapping triangles
implementation: select a diagonal that partitions the polygon into triangles
for each triangle, compute its area (e.g., 0.5 * base * height or via coordinates)
sum the triangle areas to obtain the polygon area

Distance Between Points in the Plane.name: Distance Between Points in the Plane
Distance Between Points in the Plane.description: The Euclidean distance between two points is sqrt((Δx)^2 + (Δy)^2).
cues: the solution computes a segment length from coordinate differences
coordinates of two points are known and a diagonal is formed
implementation: let Δx = x2 − x1 and Δy = y2 − y1
apply distance formula: distance = sqrt((Δx)^2 + (Δy)^2)

Aligning a Side with an Axis (Coordinate.name: Aligning a Side with an Axis (Coordinate Setup)
Aligning a Side with an Axis (Coordinate.description: Place a geometric figure so that a convenient side lies on a coordinate axis to simplify coordinate assignments.
cues: a side is chosen to lie along a coordinate axis
right-angle relationships are used to fix perpendicular directions
implementation: position a vertex at the origin
align a chosen side with the x- or y-axis
determine remaining coordinates using perpendicular relationships

Height of a Right Trapezoid.name: Height of a Right Trapezoid
Height of a Right Trapezoid.description: The height of a trapezoid is the perpendicular distance between its two parallel bases; in a right trapezoid, the perpendicular leg equals this height.
cues: figure is a trapezoid with bases parallel
there is a leg perpendicular to the bases
implementation: identify the height as the length of the segment perpendicular to both bases
use this height as the key distance in subsequent calculations

Average Rate of Change.name: Average Rate of Change

parameters.name: endpoints
parameters.description: times and distances at the interval endpoints

Average Rate of Change.description: compute the rate of change of distance with respect to time between two points on a distance–time graph to obtain average speed
cues: problem provides a distance–time graph with clearly defined start and end points
you are asked to determine an average speed over an interval
implementation: identify endpoints (t1, d1) and (t2, d2) from the graph
compute average rate: (d2 − d1) / (t2 − t1)

Slope as Speed on Distance–Time Graph.name: Slope as Speed on Distance–Time Graph

parameters.name: interval
parameters.description: start and end times of the interval

Slope as Speed on Distance–Time Graph.description: interpret the slope of a distance–time graph as speed; for an interval, the slope equals the average speed over that interval
cues: a distance–time graph is provided
you need the average speed for a specified time interval

cmath_1005.pseudocode:
We need integer n such that |n| < |n-3| < 9.

1) Solve |n-3| < 9:
   -9 < n - 3 < 9  =>  -6 < n < 12
   So n ∈ { -5, -4, -3, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, ..., 11 }.

2) Solve |n| < |n-3|:
   Since |n| and |n-3| are nonnegative, we can square:
   n^2 < (n-3)^2 = n^2 - 6n + 9
   0 < -6n + 9  =>  6n < 9  =>  n < 3/2
   So n ≤ 1 for integers.

3) Take the intersection of the two conditions:
   n ∈ { -5, -4, -3, -2, -1, 0, 1 }.

The sum of these integers is:
(-5) + (-4) + (-3) + (-2) + (-1) + 0 + 1 = -14.

Thus, the sum of all integer solutions is \boxed{-14}.

cmath_10055.pseudocode:
Let P(x) = x^{98} + x^{97} + ... + x + 1. Its roots r_1, ..., r_{98} are the 99th roots of unity other than x = 1; i.e., r_i^{99} = 1 and r_i ≠ 1.

We want S = sum_{i=1}^{98} r_i^2/(r_i + 1).

First, observe the identity
r^2/(r+1) = (r-1) + 1/(r+1),
since (r-1) + 1/(r+1) = [(r-1)(r+1) + 1]/(r+1) = r^2/(r+1).

Hence
S = sum_i (r_i - 1) + sum_i 1/(r_i + 1) = (sum_i r_i) - 98 + sum_i 1/(r_i + 1).

By Viète’s formulas, the sum of the roots of P is -1, so sum_i r_i = -1. Thus
S = -1 - 98 + sum_i 1/(r_i + 1) = -99 + sum_i 1/(r_i + 1).

To compute sum_i 1/(r_i + 1), use the standard identity for a polynomial with roots r_i:
P'(a)/P(a) = sum_i 1/(a - r_i).
Taking a = -1 gives
P'(-1)/P(-1) = sum_i 1/(-1 - r_i) = - sum_i 1/(r_i + 1),
so
sum_i 1/(r_i + 1) = - P'(-1)/P(-1).

Compute P(-1) and P'(-1) for P(x) = sum_{k=0}^{98} x^k.

- P(-1) = sum_{k=0}^{98} (-1)^k = 1.
- P'(x) = sum_{k=1}^{98} k x^{k-1}, so P'(-1) = sum_{k=1}^{98} k(-1)^{k-1}.

Pairing terms (1 - 2) + (3 - 4) + ... + (97 - 98) yields 49 pairs each contributing -1, so P'(-1) = -49.

Therefore
sum_i 1/(r_i + 1) = - P'(-1)/P(-1) = -(-49)/1 = 49.

Finally,
S = -99 + 49 = -50.

So the requested sum is \boxed{-50}.

cmath_10114.pseudocode:
Let P(x) = (a+x)(b+x)(c+x). Then P is a monic cubic:
P(x) = x^3 + (a+b+c)x^2 + (ab+bc+ca)x + abc.

Given P(1)=1, P(2)=2, P(3)=3, consider
R(x) = P(x) - x.
Then R(1)=R(2)=R(3)=0, so x-1, x-2, x-3 are roots of R. Since deg R ≤ 3 and its leading coefficient is 1, we must have
R(x) = (x-1)(x-2)(x-3).

Thus
P(x) = x + (x-1)(x-2)(x-3).

Therefore
P(4) = 4 + (4-1)(4-2)(4-3) = 4 + 3·2·1 = 10.

Hence (a+4)(b+4)(c+4) = 10. 

\boxed{10}

cmath_10132.pseudocode:
Let z = x + iy, with
z1 = 18 + 83i, z2 = 18 + 39i, z3 = 78 + 99i.

Define A = (z3 − z1)/(z2 − z1). Compute:
z3 − z1 = 60 + 16i, z2 − z1 = −44i, hence
A = (60 + 16i)/(−44i) = (−4 + 15i)/11 = a + bi with a = −4/11, b = 15/11.

Let z − z2 = (x − 18) + (y − 39)i and z − z3 = (x − 78) + (y − 99)i.
Write
B = (z − z2)/(z − z3) = (u + iv)/(s + it),
where u = x − 18, v = y − 39, s = x − 78, t = y − 99.

If AB is real, then Im(AB) = 0. Since A = a + bi, with a = −4/11, b = 15/11, we have
Im(AB) = b Re(B) + a Im(B) = 0.

Compute
Re(B) = (u s + v t)/D, Im(B) = (v s − u t)/D, with D = s^2 + t^2.

Thus
b(u s + v t) + a(v s − u t) = 0.
With a = −4/11, b = 15/11 and multiplying by 11:
15(u s + v t) − 4(v s − u t) = 0.

Substitute u, v, s, t:
u s + v t = (x − 18)(x − 78) + (y − 39)(y − 99) = x^2 + y^2 − 96x − 138y + 5265,
v s − u t = (y − 39)(x − 78) − (x − 18)(y − 99) = 60x − 60y + 1260.

Hence
15[x^2 + y^2 − 96x − 138y + 5265] − 4[60x − 60y + 1260] = 0.

Simplify:
15x^2 + 15y^2 − 1680x − 1830y + 73935 = 0,
which gives
x^2 + y^2 − 112x − 122y + 4929 = 0.

Complete the square:
(x − 56)^2 + (y − 61)^2 = 1928.

Thus the locus of z such that the given expression is real is the circle with center (56, 61) and radius sqrt(1928).

To maximize Im(z), take the topmost point on this circle:
x = 56, y = 61 + sqrt(1928).

Therefore the real part of z is Re(z) = 56, and the answer is
\boxed{56}.

cmath_10175.pseudocode:
Let P(x) = x^7 − 7, and let its roots be r_1, ..., r_7.

1) Use the resultant trick. For any u, consider Res_x(P(x), P(u − x)). Since P(u − r_i) = ∏_{j=1}^7 (u − r_i − r_j), we have
   Res_x(P(x), P(u − x)) = ∏_{i=1}^7 P(u − r_i) = ∏_{i=1}^7 ∏_{j=1}^7 (u − (r_i + r_j)) = ∏_{i,j} (u − (r_i + r_j)).

   In particular, at u = 0,
   Res_x(P(x), P(−x)) = ∏_{i,j} (−(r_i + r_j)) = (−1)^{49} ∏_{i,j} (r_i + r_j) = − ∏_{i,j} (r_i + r_j).

2) Compute the same resultant from the roots. Since P(−r_i) = (−r_i)^7 − 7 = −r_i^7 − 7 and r_i^7 = 7 (because r_i is a root), we get P(−r_i) = −14 for each i. Thus
   Res_x(P(x), P(−x)) = ∏_{i=1}^7 P(−r_i) = (−14)^7.

   Equating the two expressions for the same resultant,
   − ∏_{i,j} (r_i + r_j) = (−14)^7 ⇒ ∏_{i,j} (r_i + r_j) = 14^7.

3) Relate ∏_{i,j} (r_i + r_j) to K. The product over all ordered pairs (i, j) (i, j = 1,…,7) includes:
   - off-diagonal pairs (i ≠ j): each r_i + r_j appears twice (as (i, j) and (j, i)),
   - diagonal pairs (i = j): terms r_i + r_i = 2 r_i.

   Hence
   ∏_{i,j} (r_i + r_j) = [∏_{i<j} (r_i + r_j)]^2 · ∏_{i=1}^7 (2 r_i) = K^2 · 2^7 · ∏_{i=1}^7 r_i,

   where K = ∏_{1 ≤ i < j ≤ 7} (r_i + r_j).

4) Find ∏ r_i. For the monic polynomial x^7 − 7, the product of the roots is ∏ r_i = (−1)^7 · (−7) = 7.

5) Solve for K^2. From step 2 and 3:
   14^7 = K^2 · 2^7 · 7 ⇒ K^2 = 14^7 / (2^7 · 7) = (2^7 · 7^7) / (2^7 · 7) = 7^6.

   Therefore K^2 = 7^6 = 117649.

Answer: \boxed{117649}

cmath_10590.pseudocode:
We need n to have:
- four digits in base 3: 3^3 ≤ n ≤ 3^4 − 1, i.e., 27 ≤ n ≤ 80.
- two digits in base 6: 6^1 ≤ n ≤ 6^2 − 1, i.e., 6 ≤ n ≤ 35.

Intersection: 27 ≤ n ≤ 35.

These are consecutive integers from 27 to 35. The average of consecutive integers is (first + last)/2:
(27 + 35) / 2 = 62 / 2 = 31.

Answer: \boxed{31}

cmath_10691.pseudocode:
Let C(n) be the correct answer for item n, and S(n) the student’s answer.

- C(n) = True if n is a multiple of 4; otherwise False.
- S(n) = False if n is a multiple of 3; otherwise True.

We want the count of n in {1,2,...,100} for which C(n) = S(n).

Periodicity: C(n) depends on n mod 4 and S(n) depends on n mod 3, so the combined pattern repeats with period lcm(3,4) = 12. It suffices to analyze n = 1,...,12, then repeat 8 times (since 100 = 12*8 + 4) and handle the remaining 4 terms.

Compute for n = 1 to 12:
- C(n) is True exactly for n ∈ {4,8,12}; False otherwise.
- S(n) is False exactly for n ∈ {3,6,9,12}; True otherwise.

Matches (C(n) = S(n)) occur for n = 3, 4, 6, 8, 9. Thus there are 5 matches in each block of 12.

- Number of full 12-blocks in 1..100: 8. Matches from full blocks: 8 × 5 = 40.
- Remaining items: n = 97, 98, 99, 100 (which correspond to residues 1, 2, 3, 4 mod 12). From the 1..12 analysis, these give matches for n = 99 and 100, i.e., 2 more matches.

Total correct answers = 40 + 2 = 42.

Therefore, the final answer is \boxed{42}.

cmath_1092.pseudocode:
Let a = -8π and b = 10π. The integers n with a ≤ n ≤ b are precisely those with
⌈a⌉ ≤ n ≤ ⌊b⌋.

Compute:
- a = -8π ≈ -25.1327, so ⌈a⌉ = -25.
- b = 10π ≈ 31.4159, so ⌊b⌋ = 31.

Thus n ranges from -25 to 31 inclusive. The number of integers in [−25, 31] is
31 − (−25) + 1 = 57.

So, the number of integers n satisfying -8π ≤ n ≤ 10π is
\boxed{57}.

cmath_2171.pseudocode:
We want colorings of a 7×7 grid (49 squares) that are invariant under all symmetries of the square (rotations by multiples of 90° and reflections across the 4 symmetry axes). Call these the D4-symmetric colorings. Additionally, there must be at least one black and one white square.

Key idea: Under the action of the dihedral group D4, the squares split into orbits. A coloring that is invariant under all D4 symmetries must assign the same color to every square in each orbit. Thus the number of D4-symmetric colorings equals the number of ways to color the orbits with two colors.

Represent each square by its coordinates relative to the center. Let dx = i − 4 and dy = j − 4, so dx, dy ∈ {−3, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, 3}. Under D4, the orbit of a square is determined by the pair (|dx|, |dy|), up to order. So squares with the same unordered pair {a,b} where a = |dx| ∈ {0,1,2,3} and b = |dy| ∈ {0,1,2,3} lie in the same orbit.

Thus the number of orbits equals the number of unordered pairs {a,b} with a,b ∈ {0,1,2,3}. The count of such multisets is C(4+2−1, 2) = C(5,2) = 10.

Therefore:
- Number of D4-symmetric colorings (no restriction on colors) = 2^10 = 1024.
- Exclude the all-black and all-white colorings (to satisfy “at least one square of each color”): 1024 − 2 = 1022.

Answer: \boxed{1022}

cmath_2508.pseudocode:
Let s be the common remainder when dividing by 6 and by 8. Since the remainders must be equal, s ∈ {0,1,2,3,4,5} (because remainders mod 6 lie in 0..5).

- If n ≡ s (mod 6) and n ≡ s (mod 8) with the same s, then n − s is divisible by both 6 and 8. Hence n − s is a multiple of lcm(6,8) = 24.
- Therefore n ≡ s (mod 24) for some s ∈ {0,1,2,3,4,5}. Equivalently, n mod 24 ∈ {0,1,2,3,4,5}.

We need to count integers n with 100 < n < 200 (i.e., 101 ≤ n ≤ 199) such that n ≡ r (mod 24) for some r ∈ {0,1,2,3,4,5}.

In each block of 24 consecutive integers, there are exactly 6 numbers with residues 0,1,2,3,4,5 mod 24 (namely 24k + 0, 24k + 1, ..., 24k + 5).

Within 101 to 199, the relevant 24-blocks are for k = 4,5,6,7,8 (since 24k runs from 96 to 192, and 24k+5 runs up to 197; 24k for k=9 starts at 216 which is beyond 199). Counting:

- k = 4 block contributes only n = 101 (since 96–101 intersects the range, but only 101 has residue 0–5 mod 24).
- k = 5 block (120–125): 6 numbers (120,121,122,123,124,125).
- k = 6 block (144–149): 6 numbers.
- k = 7 block (168–173): 6 numbers.
- k = 8 block (192–197): 6 numbers.

Total = 1 + 6 + 6 + 6 + 6 = 25.

Thus, the number of integers n with 100 < n < 200 and n having the same remainder when divided by 6 and by 8 is:

\boxed{25}

cmath_3005.pseudocode:
We are given B = (12,19), C = (23,20), A = (p,q), and the median to BC has slope -5. Let M be the midpoint of BC:
- M = ((12+23)/2, (19+20)/2) = (35/2, 39/2).

Since AM has slope -5,
(q − 39/2) / (p − 35/2) = −5.
Solving gives q = 107 − 5p. (1)

The area of triangle ABC is 70. Using base BC with length √122, the height from A to BC is
h = 2·Area / base = 140 / √122.

The line BC has equation through B and C: slope 1/11, so
x − 11y + 197 = 0.

Distance from A(p,q) to BC is
h = |p − 11q + 197| / √122.

Thus |p − 11q + 197| = 140. (2)

Substitute q from (1) into (2):
p − 11(107 − 5p) + 197 = p − 1177 + 55p + 197 = 56p − 980.

So |56p − 980| = 140, which gives two solutions:
- 56p − 980 = 140 ⇒ 56p = 1120 ⇒ p = 20, then q = 107 − 5·20 = 7. So p+q = 27.
- 56p − 980 = −140 ⇒ 56p = 840 ⇒ p = 15, then q = 107 − 5·15 = 32. So p+q = 47.

The largest possible value of p+q is 47.

Therefore, the answer is \boxed{47}.

cmath_3946.pseudocode:
Let y = x^2. Then
x^8 - 98x^4 + 1 = y^4 - 98y^2 + 1.

We look for a factorization in Z[y] of the form
y^4 - 98y^2 + 1 = (y^2 + a y + 1)(y^2 - a y + 1)
because the product has no y^3 or y terms, matching the left-hand side.

Expanding:
(y^2 + a y + 1)(y^2 - a y + 1) = y^4 + (2 - a^2) y^2 + 1.

We need 2 - a^2 = -98, so a^2 = 100, hence a = 10 (or -10, which gives the same factors up to order).

Thus
y^4 - 98y^2 + 1 = (y^2 + 10y + 1)(y^2 - 10y + 1).

Returning to x with y = x^2:
x^8 - 98x^4 + 1 = (x^4 + 10x^2 + 1)(x^4 - 10x^2 + 1).

These are monic non-constant integer-coefficient polynomials. Take p(x) = x^4 + 10x^2 + 1 and q(x) = x^4 - 10x^2 + 1.

Evaluate at x = 1:
p(1) = 1 + 10 + 1 = 12,
q(1) = 1 - 10 + 1 = -8.

Thus p(1) + q(1) = 12 + (-8) = 4.

Answer: \boxed{4}

cmath_4766.pseudocode:
Let n have prime factorization n = ∏ p^{e_p}. Since 15 = 3·5, the prime exponents in 15n are:
- for p = 3: e_3(n) + 1
- for p = 5: e_5(n) + 1
- for p ≠ 3,5: e_p(n)

For 15n to be a perfect square, all these exponents must be even. Hence:
- e_3(n) is odd,
- e_5(n) is odd,
- for all p ≠ 3,5, e_p(n) is even.

This means the squarefree part of n is exactly 3·5 = 15, so n can be written as n = 15·t^2 for some integer t ≥ 1.

We need n ≤ 1000, so 15 t^2 ≤ 1000 → t^2 ≤ 1000/15 = 200/3 ≈ 66.666... ⇒ t ≤ 8.

Thus t = 1,2,...,8, giving 8 such n. (Explicitly: 15, 60, 135, 240, 375, 540, 735, 960.)

\boxed{8}

cmath_4938.pseudocode:
Let n be the largest four-digit negative integer with n ≡ 1 (mod 23).

- Write n = 1 + 23k for some integer k.
- Four-digit negative integers are those with -9999 ≤ n ≤ -1000.

Substitute n = 1 + 23k:
-9999 ≤ 1 + 23k ≤ -1000
=> -10000 ≤ 23k ≤ -1001
=> -10000/23 ≤ k ≤ -1001/23

Numerically, -10000/23 ≈ -434.78 and -1001/23 ≈ -43.52, so
k ∈ { -434, -433, ..., -44 }.

To maximize n = 1 + 23k, take the largest k in this set: k = -44.

Then n = 1 + 23(-44) = 1 - 1012 = -1011.

Thus the largest four-digit negative integer congruent to 1 mod 23 is:
\boxed{-1011}

cmath_5659.pseudocode:
Let the rectangle have coordinates D(0,0), C(8,0), B(8,4), A(0,4) so its sides are 8 by 4 cm.

- M is the midpoint of BC: B(8,4) and C(8,0) give M(8,2).
- N is the midpoint of CD: C(8,0) and D(0,0) give N(4,0).

The region AMCN is the quadrilateral with vertices A(0,4), M(8,2), C(8,0), N(4,0).

Method 1 (triangulation by diagonal AC):
- Triangle ACM has base CM of length 2 (vertical) and height from A to x = 8 is 8, so area = (1/2)(2)(8) = 8.
- Triangle ACN has base CN of length 4 (horizontal) and height from A to y = 0 is 4, so area = (1/2)(4)(4) = 8.
- Total area = 8 + 8 = 16.

Method 2 (shoelace, for verification):
Order A(0,4), M(8,2), C(8,0), N(4,0):
- Sum1 = 0*2 + 8*0 + 8*0 + 4*4 = 16
- Sum2 = 4*8 + 2*8 + 0*4 + 0*0 = 48
- Area = 1/2 |Sum1 - Sum2| = 1/2 |16 - 48| = 16

Therefore, the area of region AMCN is \boxed{16}.

cmath_5976.pseudocode:
Since ∠B and ∠C are right angles, AB ⟂ BC and BC ⟂ CD, so AB ∥ CD. Thus ABCD is a right trapezoid with height h = BC = 8.

Place coordinates for clarity:
- Let B = (0, 0) and AB lie along the x-axis. Then A = (5, 0).
- Since BC is perpendicular to AB, take C = (0, −8).
- CD ∥ AB and length CD = 20, starting at C, so D = (20, −8).

Now find AD:
AD^2 = (20 − 5)^2 + (−8 − 0)^2 = 15^2 + 8^2 = 225 + 64 = 289,
so AD = sqrt(289) = 17.

We use the coordinates given by the figure (A, B, C, D lie on a plane with right angle at D):

- A = (12,0) since AD lies on the x-axis and DC = 5 makes C = (0,5)
- C = (0,5)
- B lies on the vertical line x = 0 and AB = 15. With A = (12,0),
  AB^2 = (12)^2 + (y_B)^2 = 15^2 ⇒ 144 + y_B^2 = 225 ⇒ y_B^2 = 81 ⇒ y_B = 9

cmath_6446.pseudocode:
- The graph shows distance (in miles) vs time (in hours) from 6 a.m. to 11 a.m.
- Initial distance at 6 a.m. is 0 miles; final distance at 11 a.m. is 160 miles. (From the graph: 6 a.m. = 0 miles, 11 a.m. = 160 miles.)
- The time interval is 11 a.m. − 6 a.m. = 5 hours.
- Use the average rate of change (the slope of the distance–time graph): average speed = ΔDistance / ΔTime = (160 − 0) miles / 5 hours = 160/5 = 32 miles per hour.

Thus, the average speed from 6 a.m. to 11 a.m. is \boxed{32}.

cmath_6868.pseudocode:
Let S denote the oriented scalar triple product S = a · (b × c). The volume of the parallelepiped with edges a, b, c is |S| = 4.

We want the volume of the parallelepiped spanned by
A = a + b, B = b + 3c, C = c − 7a.

Compute the needed cross product and dot product using bilinearity and the cyclic property of the scalar triple product.

1) Expand B × C:
(b + 3c) × (c − 7a) = b × c − 7 b × a + 3 c × c − 21 c × a
= b × c + 7 a × b + 21 a × c
(since c × c = 0 and b × a = − a × b, c × a = − a × c).

2) Dot with A:
(a + b) · [b × c + 7 a × b + 21 a × c]
= a · (b × c) + b · (b × c) + 7 a · (a × b) + 7 b · (a × b)
  + 21 a · (a × c) + 21 b · (a × c).

3) Use standard identities:
- b · (b × c) = 0, a · (a × b) = 0, a · (a × c) = 0.
- b · (a × c) = − c · (a × b) = − S (cyclic permutation and the fact that c · (a × b) = S).

Thus the sum reduces to:
T = (a + b) · [(b + 3c) × (c − 7a)] = S + 0 + 0 + 0 + 0 + 21(b · (a × c))
= S + 21(− S) = −20 S.

Therefore the oriented volume is −20 times the original oriented volume, so the volume is
|T| = 20 |S| = 20 · 4 = 80.

Answer: 80

(Alternative determinant view: express the new vectors in the basis {a,b,c} as columns [1,1,0], [0,1,3], [−7,0,1]. The determinant of this 3×3 coefficient matrix is −20, so the new oriented triple product is det × S = −20 S, giving the same result.) 

\boxed{80}

cmath_8075.pseudocode:
First, recall that the domain of a square root requires a nonnegative radicand.

1) For sqrt(25 - x^2): 25 - x^2 >= 0 => x^2 <= 25 => -5 <= x <= 5.

2) For sqrt(-(x - 2)) = sqrt(2 - x): 2 - x >= 0 => x <= 2.

The domain of h(x) is the intersection of these intervals:
[-5, 5] ∩ (-∞, 2] = [-5, 2].

The width of this interval is 2 - (-5) = 7.

Therefore, the width of the domain is \boxed{7}.
